name: Carlos Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on 7B, a thirty-two-bed medical-surgical ward at the big public teaching hospital in the city, and on a day shift I've usually got six or seven patients. I start with handover at seven, scribble everything on my paper brain sheet, then it's obs, meds, wounds, drains, families and a hundred phone calls. I still do my notes by hand first and copy them into the computer later, which my charge nurse teases me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment someone who came in grey and scared walks out the door and shakes my hand. What wears me out is being one nurse short three shifts out of five and spending the last hour catching up on charting instead of sitting with people. I've been qualified five years, and the understaffing is the only thing that's never changed.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomás, who teaches music at a secondary school, in a flat we bought last year. My grandmother left me some money, so we've got a proper cushion, more than a year of bills. I'm also the ward's union steward, which mostly means I'm the one people come to when the rota is unfair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, that's what I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. At the union meeting I'd point out that every shiny system they sold us was supposed to free up nurse time, and we're still short-staffed. Online I'd share something like 'Turns out you can't automate a bed bath.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not because things are good. The ward would still be stretched, the rota would still be a mess, and the hospital would still be looking for any excuse to cut. AI being hype just means the old fight stays the old fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, paper sheet and all. I'd keep pushing the safe-staffing petition we started in the spring, aiming for every nurse on 7B to sign it. Money-wise nothing changes, we'd keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. Tired too, because the plateau still means twelve-hour shifts with not enough hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hospital looks for excuses to cut. What would that look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably buy some charting tool, call it 'efficiency', then quietly not replace the next nurse who leaves. That's happened before with the electronic records. Every new computer system on my ward came with a promise of more time with patients, and every time we ended up with less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task you'd actually be glad to hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the discharge paperwork, which eats forty minutes per patient some days. But I don't trust them to give that time back to us. They'd take it as a reason to give me an eighth patient.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **hype** proves new systems never fix **short staffing**.
I'd post that you **can't automate** a bed bath, half as a joke.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but the ward's real problem, **understaffing**, would stay exactly the same.
I suspect management would still use any small **time saving** as a reason to cut.
do: Keep working with my **paper brain sheet** and charting the same way I do now.
Push the **safe-staffing petition** until every nurse on 7B has signed it.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** a little each month, as we already do.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a smug streak about being right on the hype.
Still **tired**, because twelve-hour shifts with too few hands carry on.
S0.quote: Every new computer system on my ward came with a promise of more time with patients, and every time we ended up with less.
fieldNote: His calm comes from **secure pay** and savings, not from liking how the ward runs.
He sees every technology through the lens of **staffing ratios** and management motives.
As union steward, his first move in any world is a **collective** one, never a personal one.

steps.text: Keep the paper handover sheet and usual charting routine on 7B
Collect signatures from every nurse on 7B for the safe-staffing petition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds more like what the tech people keep promising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: fine, let it write the notes, but don't touch the ratios. I'd bring it up at the union branch, because this is exactly the kind of change that needs rules before it lands, not after. With friends I'd probably say nurses are safe and office workers should worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is safe, but the job around me gets worse. The ward clerk and the discharge coordinator are the ones who'd go, and their work lands on us. I'd hate the new systems, and I'd be the slowest one on the ward to learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement that any AI charting tool can't be used to raise patient numbers per nurse. I'd do the minimum training they make compulsory, and no more. We'd keep our savings where they are, because I don't see my pay changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Annoyed that I'll have to learn things I didn't ask for. But not scared for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline, our ward clerk, who's been there twenty-two years and knows every consultant's quirks. If a computer starts booking the scans and chasing the porters, Pauline (our ward clerk) is gone, and her work lands on the nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the minimum training. What if the ward starts relying on the new tools and you fall behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll be the guy asking the student nurse how to click the button, which I already am, to be honest. I'd learn it when I have to. I just won't pretend to be excited.

say: I'd say AI can **write the notes** but must never change nurse-to-patient **ratios**.
I'd tell friends that **office workers**, not nurses, are the ones who should worry.
think: I think my own **job is safe**, but the work around it gets heavier.
I expect **ward clerks** and coordinators to go first, with their tasks landing on nurses.
I'd be the **slowest learner** on the ward and resent the new systems.
do: Push the union for a **written agreement** that AI tools can't raise patient numbers.
Do only the **compulsory training** on any new charting system, and nothing extra.
Leave our **savings** untouched, since I don't expect my pay to change.
feel: **Uneasy** and irritated about learning tools nobody asked for.
Not **scared** for his own job, but worried for support staff.
S1.quote: If a computer starts booking the scans and chasing the porters, Pauline (our ward clerk) is gone, and her work lands on the nurses.
fieldNote: He separates his own **job security** clearly from worries about the ward clerk.
His resistance to technology is **open and unapologetic**, even a bit proud.
He frames AI entirely as a **bargaining issue** for the union, not a personal one.

steps.text: Table a motion at the union branch banning AI-driven increases in patient numbers
Finish only the compulsory e-learning module on the new charting tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's a lot faster than anything I've thought about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: nobody wants a robot holding their mum's hand when she's dying. At the union I'd want an emergency motion, because if thinking AI arrives in 2028 then the planning and the charting go first, and that changes how they staff the ward. Online I'd probably get angry at the tech billionaires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared for the first time. In 2028 the thinking parts of my job, the care plans, the drug checks, the handover, all go to the machine. Then in 2031 a robot can turn a patient, and management will ask why they need seven nurses on a shift when four plus robots will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put more into savings, maybe an extra four hundred a month, and stop the plans for a new car. I'd work with the union nationally on safe-staffing laws, writing to my local representative and getting people to the march. I'd still refuse to use the AI myself unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Angry that it's being done to us. Weirdly a bit protective of the patients, like they're going to be left alone with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AI in 2028 and robots in 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd probably still have work in 2028, but I'd be doing the lifting while the computer does the thinking. By 2031 I'd be thirty-one, a nurse who hates computers, competing with a robot that never takes a sick day. That's the bit that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got more than a year of savings and plenty of hospitals nearby. Does that change how worried you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps. Tomás and I wouldn't be on the street. But every hospital would be buying the same robots at the same time, so 'plenty of jobs nearby' stops meaning much.

say: I'd say nobody wants a **robot** at the bedside of someone who's **dying**.
I'd call for an **emergency union motion**, because charting and planning go first in 2028.
think: I'd be **scared** for the first time, as care plans and drug checks move to machines.
I expect management to cut from **seven nurses** to four once robots arrive in **2031**.
do: Save an **extra 400 a month** and cancel plans to buy a new car.
Write to my **local representative** and get colleagues to a **safe-staffing march**.
Keep **refusing** to use the AI myself unless the hospital makes it compulsory.
feel: **Anxious** and angry that the change is being done to nurses.
**Protective** of patients he imagines left alone with machines.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be thirty-one, a nurse who hates computers, competing with a robot that never takes a sick day.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** to robots gave him little comfort; he sees it as borrowed time.
Strong savings soften but don't remove the fear, because every hospital **buys robots** at once.
He still won't touch AI himself, so his **resistance** may cost him in the thinking years.

steps.text: Move an extra 400 a month into savings and cancel the new car
Bring colleagues from 7B to the national safe-staffing march
Write to the local representative asking for legal nurse ratios

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's when I'd be thirty-two. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get the rules in place, while there's still time. At work I'd be the one handing out leaflets about ratios and asking the union to fight for a say over how robots get used. With friends I'd probably say the same stuff about tech billionaires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to save and to see which wards keep human nurses longest. I reckon the hands-on wards, like mine, last a bit longer than outpatient desk jobs. But I don't really believe the hospital will protect anyone just because there was warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving the extra money but not go crazy, maybe three hundred a month. I'd get more involved in the union's national committee on technology, because if I'm going to stay a nurse I want a say over the robots. I wouldn't retrain into anything techy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Less frightened than with two years, more like a long dread in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the years before 2031, while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to fight, honestly. Five years is long enough to get a law that says a robot can't count as a nurse on the rota. If we lose that fight, then I'd think about what next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay a nurse. What if the hospital offers training in running the AI systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably let the younger ones take it. That sounds selfish, but I didn't become a nurse to stare at dashboards. I'd only go if it was that or lose my job.

say: I'd say this is the time to put **rules** in place, while there's still **warning**.
I'd hand out leaflets asking for a union **say over robots** on the ward.
think: Five years lets me **save** and watch which wards keep **human nurses** longest.
I think hands-on wards last longer, but don't trust the **hospital** to protect anyone.
do: Keep saving an **extra 300 a month**, without cutting our life back hard.
Join the union's **national technology committee** to shape how robots get used.
**Turn down** any move into technical or AI-focused nursing roles.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a long dread in the background rather than sharp fear.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to get a law that says a robot can't count as a nurse on the rota.
fieldNote: Extra warning time turns his fear into a **campaign plan** rather than personal change.
He puts his hope in a **law** stopping robots counting as nurses on the rota.
He openly admits he'd leave **AI training** to younger colleagues, aware it sounds selfish.

steps.text: Set up a standing transfer of 300 a month into savings
Apply for a seat on the union's national technology committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's 2039 for the robots. I'd be thirty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for treating nurses badly. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone who'd listen. I'd probably be less loud online, because ten years sounds far away to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd mostly be okay. By 2036 I'd maybe be a senior nurse, and by 2039, with savings and the flat mostly paid, I'd have options. The real risk is that I sit back for nine years and then get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep going. I'd stay on the union side of things, because a decade of warning is exactly when unions can win something. I'd maybe look at a specialist course in tissue viability, wound care, in a few years, since it's the most hands-on thing I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A bit uneasy about the end point, but I've got a decade and a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is sitting back. Do you think you would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'm the nurse who still writes notes on paper, so give me ten years of warning and I'll use nine of them pretending it isn't coming. Tomás would nag me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything at home, with Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about it. Tomás teaches, and the thinking AI would reach his job in 2036, before robots reach mine. So weirdly, I might be the safer earner in our house, which I've never been.

say: I'd say a **decade of warning** leaves no excuse for treating nurses badly.
I'd speak up at **union meetings** but stay quieter online, as ten years sounds far off.
think: I think I'd **mostly be okay**, with savings and the flat mostly paid by 2039.
My real risk is **sitting back** for nine years and getting caught out.
do: Carry on **nursing as normal** on 7B for the next several years.
Keep up **union work**, since a decade is when unions can win something.
Consider a **wound care course** in a few years, as the most hands-on skill.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a little unease about the **end point**.
S4.quote: I'm the nurse who still writes notes on paper, so give me ten years of warning and I'll use nine of them pretending it isn't coming.
fieldNote: He honestly predicts his own **procrastination**, which is unusual self-awareness.
He notices his partner's **teaching job** meets thinking AI before his own job meets robots.
His calm rests on **savings and housing**, while the end point still nags at him.

steps.text: Keep working day shifts on 7B without changing roles
Stay on as union steward and push for long-term staffing deals
Wait until about 2030 before deciding on a wound care course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to fight for rules before it lands. What would help is a law on safe staffing that says a robot doesn't count as a nurse, and a union with real power over how the machines get used. Give us a law that keeps a human nurse at every bedside, and I'll stop worrying about the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about patients. Everyone talks about our jobs, but the people in those beds don't get a vote on whether a machine turns them at three in the morning. Somebody should ask them.

headlineQuote: Give us a law that keeps a human nurse at every bedside, and I'll stop worrying about the robots.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** ward nurse and union steward on a busy public **medical-surgical ward**.
He lives with partner Tomás in a new flat, backed by **over a year** of savings from an inheritance.
He **refuses** to use AI and still writes notes on paper, and says so proudly.
He reads every scenario through **staffing ratios**, answering with union action rather than personal change.
He stays calm or uneasy except for **AGI by 2028**, where fast robots make him anxious.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, leaving **no time** to win rules before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A **safe-staffing law** saying a robot never counts as a nurse on the rota.
A union with **real power** over how hospitals bring in machines.
